extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the 'markedly different characteristics' comparison used to determine whether a claimed nature-based product is a product-of-nature exception for patent eligibility under Step 2A. Covers when to apply the analysis, how to select natural counterparts, what characteristics to compare, and how to evaluate marked differences with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations in a claim. If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, the analysis is unnecessary because it is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product; if the nature-based product is not naturally occurring (e.g., due to human intervention), then perform the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overly extend the analysis to claim elements that are not nature-based. The analysis is targeted to nature-based product limitations whether claimed alone or as part of a larger claim. Examples: a claim to 'a Lactobacillus bacterium' requires the analysis; a claim including Lactobacillus plus non-nature elements requires analyzing only the Lactobacillus limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim is to a nature-based product by itself, apply the analysis to the entire claimed product. When the claim is to a nature-based product produced by combining multiple components, apply the analysis to the resultant combination rather than the components separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chakrabarty applied the analysis to an entire genetically modified bacterium. For a probiotic composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk, analyze the mixture for markedly different characteristics, not Lactobacillus and milk individually. If the claim is a nature-based product in combination with non-nature elements (e.g., a kit with instructions), analyze only the nature-based product limitation; other elements are evaluated separately in Prong Two or Step 2B if needed. Funk Bros. illustrates analyzing only the bacterial mixture component in a claim with other non-nature parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For product-by-process claims, the analysis turns on whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2113 for additional product-by-process guidance. The focus is on the product as recited, not necessarily on the process steps, when assessing marked differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims — general rule and exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, process claims are not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis because process claims focus on active steps rather than products. However, if a process claim is drafted such that it is substantively indistinguishable from a product claim (i.e., focuses on the product), then apply the markedly different characteristics analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example exceptions: a claim drafted as 'a method of providing an apple' is effectively directed to the apple (a nature-based product) and should be treated like a product claim. Claims that merely identify naturally occurring matter (e.g., detecting cffDNA) can be treated as claims to the natural product and thus be subject to the analysis (Ariosa/Sequenom example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility outcome based on marked differences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart, then the claim does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B) unless the claim recites another exception. If the entire claim is a single nature-based product and a marked difference is shown, no further Step 2B analysis is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics, it is a product-of-nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two (integration into a practical application) and possibly Step 2B. For claims including additional elements, examiners should check whether other exceptions are recited and proceed accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to compare against the claimed nature-based product. If the claimed product is derived from a natural thing, the natural precursor is typically the counterpart; do not substitute broader adjacent natural material (e.g., use a gene rather than the whole chromosome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple natural counterparts exist, select the closest counterpart based on the examiner's expertise in the art (e.g., pick the most closely related breed for a cloned animal). For combinations with no natural counterpart mixture, compare to the individual natural components. Best practice: when issuing an ineligibility rejection, identify the selected counterpart in the Office action if the record is unclear to aid applicant response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying appropriate characteristics for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify characteristics to compare that are actually possessed by the claimed product, based on the claim language and the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of that claim. Characteristics can be structural, functional, or other properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics relied on must be recited in the claim or encompassed by the claim's BRI; unclaimed characteristics cannot be used to establish marked differences. Example: a claim to 'deoxyribose' implies structural characteristics (loss of a hydroxyl). For 'isolated gene B' rely on what that term reasonably encompasses (sequence, encoded protein, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of characteristics to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate characteristics include the product's structure, function, and/or other properties (biological/pharmacological functions, chemical/physical properties, phenotype, genetic or physical structure/form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting examples provided by the courts: biological/pharmacological functions (protein-encoding info; binding ability; bacterial infectivity; ability to degrade hydrocarbons; vitamin C preventing scurvy), chemical/physical properties (alkalinity; ductility/malleability), phenotypic features (shape, size, color, behavior), and structure/form (physical plasmids; chemical nonsalt/crystalline form; nucleotide sequence; genotype). Use these categories to frame the comparison on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for evaluating whether a characteristic is 'markedly different'
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic is 'markedly different' only if it is changed compared to the natural counterpart and is not an inherent/innate or incidental characteristic of the natural counterpart. The change generally must have been caused or produced by the applicant's efforts or influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product is a product-of-nature exception. If at least one characteristic is changed and that change was produced by the applicant, the change will generally be considered markedly different such that the claimed product is not a product-of-nature exception. Incidental differences from isolation or unclaimed phenotypic variation do not generally qualify (see Myriad, Ambry, Roslin, and Marden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products found to have markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples where claimed products were held to have markedly different characteristics and thus were eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty: genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids and ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons was markedly different and eligible. Myriad: full-length cDNA (exon-only sequence) was structurally distinct from genomic DNA and held not a product of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products lacking markedly different characteristics (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples where claimed products lacked marked differences and were held to be products-of-nature exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad: isolated but otherwise unchanged genomic BRCA genes — isolation alone was incidental and insufficient. Ambry: primers (single-stranded DNA corresponding to natural sequences) retained the same sequence and innate binding function — not markedly different. Marden: ductility of vanadium is inherent, not conferred by a new combination. Roslin: cloned animals that are genetic replicas lacked markedly different characteristics; unclaimed phenotypic differences cannot establish marked difference. These illustrate that mere isolation, synthetically creating the same sequence, or unclaimed/innate properties typically do not establish marked differences.
